source: Ma, Grandi et al. (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models
finding: GPT-3 solutions for 12 design problems were rated by experts as more feasible and useful, but less novel, than crowdsourced solutions. Crowd sets had higher variance.
numbers: 12 design problems; 5 GPT-3 solution sets per problem (base, zero-shot with unique/novel/diverse adjective, few-shot) vs an Amazon Mechanical Turk set; expert ratings on 0-2 scales for feasibility, novelty, usefulness.
limits: One old model (GPT-3). Small expert rating effort. Text ideas only. Does not use the full Shah et al. quantity/variety/quality/novelty set.
agent_relevance: Shows the early LLM profile: quality up, novelty down. An agent should score novelty and variety separately from feasibility.

source: Ma, Grandi et al. (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models
finding: Prompt wording moved embedding similarity to the human set a lot, and unpredictably. Adding the word 'diverse' raised similarity on one problem and lowered it on another.
numbers: Mean nearest-generated-sample cosine similarity to human set: base 0.748, zero-shot unique 0.746, novel 0.775, diverse 0.779, few-shot 0.804 (SD 0.06). Problem 2 with 'diverse': 0.627 to 0.805. Problem 11 with 'diverse': 0.738 to 0.675.
limits: Similarity to humans is a coverage measure, not quality. 12 problems, no significance test across prompts.
agent_relevance: A fixed 'be diverse' instruction is not a reliable lever. Measure the set, do not trust the instruction.

source: Ma, Grandi et al. (2023) Conceptual design generation using large language models
finding: Breadth of the idea set (convex hull volume in embedding space, their novelty proxy) was highest for humans. Few-shot and the 'novel' adjective made LLM sets narrower because GPT-3 repeated ideas with small wording changes.
numbers: Convex hull volume: crowd 0.294 (SD 0.03); GPT-3 zero-shot 'unique' 0.266 (SD 0.1); few-shot 0.2 (SD 0.04); zero-shot 'novel' 0.186 (SD 0.07). GPT-3 repeats the same idea after a few outputs when asked for 100.
limits: Convex hull is sensitive to outliers and dimension. Single model, single embedding (SentenceBERT).
agent_relevance: Repetition inside one long generation is a real failure. Many short independent samples plus dedup should beat one long list.

source: Miao et al. (2024) Diamond of Thought: a design-thinking framework for LLMs in wearable design
finding: Authors adapted the Shah et al. four metrics. They dropped quantity because every group had to deliver a fixed number of concepts, and scored novelty, variety and quality (split into rationality and completeness). A staged design-thinking scaffold (DoT) beat input-output and chain-of-thought prompting.
numbers: Four conditions (input-output, CoT, DoT, human designers) on four wearable design tasks; 6 expert raters; Kendall W: rationality 1.00, integrality 0.90, novelty 0.91, variety 0.91. Score order IO < CoT < DoT; DoT vs human total difference p = 0.89 (not significant).
limits: Very small sample, one domain (wearables, embodied cognition). The DoT used a domain case database.
agent_relevance: Direct use of the Shah metric set on an LLM scaffold. A staged design process plus a case database lifted rationality and completeness, but not novelty.

source: Miao et al. (2024) Diamond of Thought: a design-thinking framework for LLMs in wearable design
finding: Humans still led on novelty and variety. DoT led on rationality and completeness.
numbers: DoT vs humans: rationality p = 0.025, completeness p = 0.039, innovation p = 0.017 (humans higher), variety p = 0.350 (not significant, small gap). Judges guessed 'human author' for IO 50%, CoT 41.6%, DoT 62.5%, humans 70.8%.
limits: Small N, authors admit low power. Guess rates from few interviews.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can raise quality-type scores without closing the novelty gap. Keep novelty as a separate target.

source: Sankar and Sen (2025) A novel mathematical framework for objective characterization of ideas through vector embeddings in LLM
finding: Proposes to replace human-rated variety and novelty with embedding geometry: embed ideas, then use UMAP, DBSCAN clusters and PCA eigenvalues to measure spread and redundancy of an idea set. Built for LLM-generated idea sets.
numbers: Six product design problems, 100 ideas each, compared against five AI scorers. Variety is the Shah et al. set-level breadth measure.
limits: Weakly validated against human judgement. Embedding and cluster settings change the answer.
agent_relevance: A cheap, code-computable stand-in for the Shah variety score. Fits guardrail G5 (code selects).

source: Sankar and Sen (2025) A novel mathematical framework for objective characterization of ideas through vector embeddings in LLM
finding: Five AI novelty scorers (GPT-based, OCSAI, AIDE, CLAUS, SemDis) disagreed with each other on the same 100 ideas per problem, and none used the low end of the scale.
numbers: Mean novelty on 1-5 scale: AIDE 3.83 (SD 0.31), CLAUS 3.43 (SD 0.2), GPT 3.32, SemDis 3.09, OCSAI 2.28 (SD 0.7). No method scored below about 2.
limits: No common human gold set used here. Single study.
agent_relevance: Model-graded novelty has compressed range and scorer-specific bias. Do not use one LLM grade as the novelty measure.

source: Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of large language models on human creative ideation
finding: With ChatGPT as the idea aid, different people ended up with more similar ideas than with a card-deck aid, but each person's own ideas were not narrower.
numbers: N = 36 recruited, 33 analysed, within-subject. Group-level distance to mean idea embedding: ChatGPT 0.24 (SD .07) vs Oblique Strategies 0.28 (SD .08), t(32) = 2.15, p = 0.038, d = 0.47. Individual level: 0.65 vs 0.66, p = 0.352.
limits: Small N, one tool pair, mixed ChatGPT 3.5 versions, embedding validated only in a small side test.
agent_relevance: Homogenization is a set-level property across users or runs. An agent running many sessions needs a set-level diversity check, not a per-answer check.

source: Anderson, Shah and Kreminski (2024) Homogenization effects of large language models on human creative ideation
finding: ChatGPT users produced more ideas and more elaborated ideas, but felt less responsible for them.
numbers: Idea count 8.39 (SD 3.39) vs 7.32 (SD 3.22), about +15%, t(32) = 2.10, p = 0.044, d = 0.32. Stoplisted word count 8.25 vs 6.46. Self-assigned responsibility 48.17% vs 63.63%, t(32) = 3.21, p = 0.003, d = 0.67.
limits: Quality was not rated. Fluency gain is small.
agent_relevance: Quantity and elaboration rose while set-level originality fell: the Shah metrics move in different directions, so report all of them.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review found LLM research ideas more novel than expert-written ideas, and slightly less feasible.
numbers: 49 expert writers, 79 expert reviewers, 298 reviews, 7 topics, 49 ideas per condition. Novelty: human 4.84, AI 5.64 (p < 0.01), AI plus human rerank 5.81 (p < 0.001). Excitement 4.55 vs 5.19. Feasibility 6.61 vs 6.34 (not significant).
limits: Idea format normalised by LLM; novelty judged without execution. Reviewer agreement only 56.1% (balanced accuracy).
agent_relevance: Expert novelty ratings are noisy, so treat a measured gain with care. Supports over-generate-and-rank.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Generating more ideas did not give more distinct ideas. After embedding dedup the pool plateaued.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas per topic; duplicate = cosine similarity above 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2); only about 200 non-duplicate ideas per topic remained (about 5%).
limits: One agent and one embedding; threshold set by manual inspection.
agent_relevance: The quantity metric saturates. Stop sampling by the non-duplicate rate, not by a fixed count.

source: Si, Yang and Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs generate novel research ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: LLM judges were no better than humans at scoring ideas, and worse than the already low human agreement.
numbers: Human split-half agreement 56.1%. Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker 53.3%; GPT-4o direct 50.0%, GPT-4o pairwise 45.0%, Claude-3.5 direct 51.7%. Claude-3.5 zero-shot ranker on ICLR review data 71.4%, GPT-4o 61.1%.
limits: Ranker built as a proxy from public review data; ideas judged at ideation stage only.
agent_relevance: Do not let a model grade its own ideas for novelty. Matches G5.

source: Si, Hashimoto and Yang (2025) The ideation-execution gap: execution outcomes of LLM-generated versus human research ideas
finding: When experts actually executed the ideas, the novelty advantage of LLM ideas disappeared.
numbers: N = 43 experts, over 100 hours each. Score change after execution (1-10 scale): human ideas novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052; LLM ideas -1.049, -1.760, -1.879 (differences p < 0.05). Rankings flipped on many metrics.
limits: Small N (43 projects). NLP prompting-style research only.
agent_relevance: Idea metrics measured before testing overstate LLM idea value. Pair ideation metrics with a test-based outcome (G3).

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: Pools of GPT-4 product ideas were less diverse than a pool from human students. Chain-of-thought brainstorming came close to the human pool.
numbers: Mean pairwise cosine similarity (lower is more diverse): human student group 0.243; CoT 0.255; Steve Jobs persona about 0.37; base prompt about 0.38-0.39; other prompts up to 0.432. 35 prompts, 10 sessions of 100 ideas each vs 100 MBA student ideas.
limits: One task (college-student product under $50), GPT-4 only. Abstract and table give slightly different base values (0.377 vs 0.386). Working paper.
agent_relevance: The best prompt-level fix for low variety was a multi-step procedure, not a persona. Supports pooled independent runs with dedup.

source: Meincke, Mollick and Terwiesch (2024) Prompting diverse ideas: increasing AI idea variance
finding: Chain-of-thought also enlarged the number of distinct ideas the model can reach before running dry.
numbers: Estimated unique ideas about 3700 for the base prompt vs about 4700 for CoT. Hybrid brainstorming (40 sessions x 30 ideas, groups of 4 pick best 10) also tested.
limits: Estimate from exhaustion curves with a cosine uniqueness threshold.
agent_relevance: Quantity-until-exhaustion is a usable metric for an agent's stopping rule.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: A single model repeats itself on open-ended questions even at high temperature and with min-p decoding.
numbers: 70+ models, 26K real open-ended queries (Infinity-Chat). 50 samples per query on 100 queries; at top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0 average pairwise similarity of same-prompt answers typically above 0.8. Min-p (temp 2.0): 81% of pairs above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8.
limits: Embedding similarity (text-embedding-3-small) is not human-rated novelty. Random cross-prompt pairs sit at 0.1-0.2, only a scale reference.
agent_relevance: Sampling knobs do not buy variety. Variety must come from structure: different frames, constraints or operators.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: Different models give nearly the same answers, so sampling several vendor models does not give independent ideas. Reward models and LLM judges also match human ratings less well where people disagree.
numbers: Cross-model average pairwise similarity 0.71 to 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 and qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 and gpt-4o 0.81. 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item.
limits: Cause of shared outputs unknown (shared or synthetic data).
agent_relevance: Strong support for G4: model ensembles do not fix variety.

source: Hou et al. (2026) CreativityPrism: a cross-domain evaluation framework for LLM creativity
finding: Quality, novelty and diversity are separate axes of LLM creativity. Big models win on quality but not on divergent thinking.
numbers: 17 LLMs, 8 tasks in 3 domains. Overall: GPT4.1 .695, Llama3.3-70B .641, small models .40-.46. Frontier models lead open models by .10 (15%) on creative writing and logical reasoning, but no significant lead in divergent thinking. Temperature 0.75.
limits: Automatic judges; main table from one run. Novelty definitions differ by task.
agent_relevance: Report novelty and diversity apart from quality, as Shah et al. do. A single creativity score hides trade-offs.

source: Hou et al. (2026) CreativityPrism: a cross-domain evaluation framework for LLM creativity
finding: Novelty metrics barely agree with each other across tasks; diversity and quality metrics do agree.
numbers: Pearson r between model scores on some novelty metrics as low as -0.25 (Surprise in short stories vs Divergence@0 in NeoCoder). Within-task correlations 0.84 or higher for TTCT.
limits: Only 17 models, so correlations are rough.
agent_relevance: Novelty has no single definition. Our agent needs a task-specific novelty check, not a general one.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: On standard divergent-thinking tests, LLM answers are individually about as original as human ones, but the population of LLM answers is far less varied.
numbers: 22 LLMs (7 one-per-family in tests) vs humans N = 102 on Alternative Uses, Forward Flow, Divergent Association. AUT originality LLM 0.711 vs human 0.696 (p = 0.001, effect 0.1). Population variability LLM 0.459 vs human 0.738 (effect 2.2) after matching answer length.
limits: Prolific sample scored lower on individual originality than earlier studies. Default system prompt in main tests.
agent_relevance: Individual novelty and set variety dissociate. Matches Shah: score the set, not only items.

source: Wenger and Kenett (2025) We're different, we're the same: creative homogeneity across LLMs
finding: Telling the model to be creative raised individual originality and variability a little, but variability stayed far below humans.
numbers: Variability: baseline 0.459, 'more creative' 0.503, 'very creative' (with a $200 reward line) 0.576, 'not creative' 0.492; human 0.738. Originality: baseline 0.711 to 'very creative' 0.754.
limits: One task (AUT), one prompt family.
agent_relevance: Instruction-only fixes close less than half the gap. Needs structural methods.

source: Ashkinaze et al. (2025) How AI ideas affect the creativity, diversity and evolution of human ideas
finding: Showing people many ChatGPT ideas before they brainstormed raised the diversity of the whole pool but did not change how creative each idea was.
numbers: 844 participants, 48 countries, 3414 responses. High-exposure diversity vs control: Cliff's delta 0.31 (disclosed) and 0.26 (undisclosed), both p = 0.001. Low exposure: only undisclosed, delta 0.11. Individual creativity: no difference, F(4, 19.86) = 0.12, p = 0.97.
limits: Five prompts; online volunteers; diversity is cosine distance. Opposite sign to the homogenization findings, so it depends on the comparison baseline.
agent_relevance: Seeding with outside ideas can raise set variety, relevant if the agent draws on a stored idea bank.

source: Dong and Yakura (2026) Human diversity fuels collective creativity that large language models cannot simulate or sustain
finding: AI-supplied ideas shrank the collective pool, AI only polishing human ideas did not, and persona-simulated pools stayed below every human pool at any temperature.
numbers: Preregistered metaphor experiment, native vs non-native English writers. Pool contraction (centroid similarity): AI ideation b = 0.036 (p < 0.001); AI refinement b = 0.007 (p = 0.516). Simulated pools (GPT-4o mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Qwen3.5-27b, temp 0.5-2.0): diversity plateaued near 0.50, gap of 0.04 to the least diverse human pool.
limits: Preprint, not peer reviewed. One task type (metaphors).
agent_relevance: Where the model enters matters: use it to refine and test, not as the only idea source.

source: Sternlicht et al. (2026) Old ideas, novel problems: the instability of LLM-based novelty evaluation
finding: LLM novelty judges flip on small prompt changes. Retrieval and more reasoning help little.
numbers: Six judges, pairs from OpenReview with unanimous reviewer labels. One prompt sentence about reviewers shifts pairwise accuracy by over 50 points for gpt-5.4 (52.6-point gap between prompts P3 and P4; the two prompts disagree on 55.8% of pairs). Tie rate up to 35% for claude-opus-4-6. Below chance on LLM-generated ideas for some judges.
limits: Reviewer-acceptance proxy for novelty. Idea pairs from one generator.
agent_relevance: Strong warning against LLM-judged novelty without calibration. Use code metrics and held-out checks.

source: Padmakumar et al. (2026) Measuring LLM novelty as the frontier of original and high-quality output
finding: Defines novelty as the harmonic mean of unseen n-gram fraction and a quality score. Scale and post-training raise novelty through quality. Prompting and novel in-context examples raise originality but cost quality.
numbers: OLMo, OLMo-2, Pythia families; story completion, poetry, creative tool use. Some base LLM text is less novel than human web text.
limits: Open-data models only. Novelty tied to training-data n-grams.
agent_relevance: A combined metric that blocks novel-but-useless output. Template for a novelty score gated by a pass check.

source: Doudkin et al. (2025) The Spark Effect: engineering creative diversity in multi-agent AI systems
finding: Ten curated role personas as separate agents raised judged diversity a lot over one generic prompt. A first, generic multi-agent version did not.
numbers: LLM-as-judge 1-10 scale, 7 tasks: baseline 3.14; v1 3.76 (+0.61, t(6) = 0.77, p = 0.47, d = 0.29); Spark v2 7.90 (+5.69 over baseline, t(6) = 7.61, p = 2.68e-4, d = 2.88); human experts 8.90. Judge scored human answers 10.22, an optimism bias of +1.32.
limits: Industry white paper, LLM judge, 7 tasks, no peer review. Contradicts the Dong result on simulated pools.
agent_relevance: Persona agents may add judged variety, but the judge is biased and G4 says persona voters are not independent. A lead to test, not a design.

source: Exploring design of multi-agent LLM dialogues for research ideation (2025)
finding: More critics and more critique-revision turns raised the share of non-duplicate ideas, with diminishing returns after three turns.
numbers: Non-duplicate ratio: single pass 0.69, baseline self-critique 0.77, three critics 0.80. Depth: three turns 0.85 with Precision@10 0.52; a fourth turn gave no more.
limits: Scored with embedding dedup and a GPT-4 tournament judge; one idea domain.
agent_relevance: A concrete stopping rule: stop revising when the non-duplicate ratio stops rising (about 3 rounds).

source: Analogical LLM Ideation Agent (ALIA) study (2025) Leveraging LLMs for design ideation
finding: A speech-driven LLM agent supplied synectics-style analogical stimuli to design teams. Participants rated their own ideas better with the tool.
numbers: Small group ideation sessions, AI-assisted vs traditional; preliminary, self-rated.
limits: Self-rated outcomes only, no independent variety or novelty score. Only abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: An LLM agent loop built on a classic design ideation method (synectics, analogy).

source: Sorensen et al. (2026) Axiom-based aggregation functions for ideation metrics (Design Science)
finding: Argues that common ways of adding up Shah-style quality, quantity, novelty and variety into set scores are flawed and proposes axiom-based aggregation, with AI evaluation in mind.
numbers: Not read; known only from a search summary.
limits: Not opened, treat as a lead.
agent_relevance: Check before choosing how to aggregate idea scores into a set score.
